Mini-activity: design one safe merge


1 Which plan safely combines a person-level file with a day-level file?  A. Merge many-to-many on participant ID, then remove rows that look duplicated  B. Define the day-level output grain, verify each source key, declare many days to one person/recording, anticipate unmatched records, and merge only after both key tests pass  C. Drop unmatched records before checking whether they represent expected missingness  D. Rename both ID columns to the same name and assume that proves uniqueness





Check answer


Reset and retry






Completion evidence: the file inventory and dictionary allow a collaborator to find the exact original column and reproduce every renamed or derived variable.



Practice


Self-check with Feedback



1 Which Part 4 night file should normally start the sleep-analysis dataset?  A. The full QC file, with every excluded night silently restored  B. Any Part 4 file whose filename is shortest  C. results/part4_nightsummary_sleep_cleaned.csv  D. A participant-level Part 5 activity file




2 The analysis plan requires 10-minute MVPA bouts. What should happen first?  A. Always recreate the bouts in Stata, regardless of the GGIR configuration  B. Verify mvpadur, boutdur.mvpa, and the output columns before deciding whether a new derivation is needed  C. Treat every 10-minute clock interval as an MVPA bout  D. Use the 10-hour valid-day rule as the bout definition




3 May a course/project L40/M100/V400 file be appended to a file with different L/M/V values as though both estimate the same outcomes?  A. Yes, whenever the column names match  B. Yes, after deleting the threshold values from the filenames  C. Yes, if the two files have the same number of rows  D. No; trace the configurations and keep the methods separate unless an explicit analysis compares them




4 Why is participant ID alone usually insufficient as the key for a day-level file?  A. One participant normally has multiple days, so the key also needs the verified day/date or window identifier  B. Participant IDs are never allowed in research data  C. Every day-level table must instead use row number as its permanent key  D. The participant ID becomes unique after sorting the table





Check answers


Reset and retry

Module 6 video: cleaning GGIR outputs and standardizing variables.




Quick summary Review aid


Identify the participant-, day-, and night-level GGIR outputs before merging, and read thresholds encoded in part 5 file names as part of the analysis method. Apply only approved sleep and bout rules, then standardize variables in a data dictionary that preserves source, unit, transformation, and missing-value decisions.





Read the full video transcript Timestamped · English


Download English captions (.vtt)



00:00 Welcome to Module 6, Cleaning and Standardizing. In this lesson you will learn how to identify the observation unit of each GGIR output, interpret processing information recorded in file names, apply approved cleaning rules, construct cumulative bout measures, and standardize


00:15 variables while preserving traceability. We will connect these concepts to practice through a short Stata demonstration. Module 5 was about checking data quality. We reviewed the quality control outputs, inspected plots and reports, and documented which records should be


00:30 kept, reviewed, or excluded. Module 6 starts only after those decisions are documented. Here we apply the approved rules to the GGIR outputs, clean night and day-level records, standardize variable names and labels, and preserve a traceable record of every transformation. We are not yet building


00:48 the final analysis dataset, combining source files, calculating final participant-level outcomes, and creating the analysis-ready Stata dataset come in Module 7. This boundary matters. Module 5 decides, Module 6 cleans and standardizes, and Module 7 integrates the approved outputs.


01:08 Before cleaning or merging any GGIR table, always ask one question. What does one row represent? In part2_summary, one row represents one participant or recording file. Therefore, ID alone should uniquely identify each row. In part2_daysummary, the same participant


01:25 can appear on several calendar dates. Here, one row represents one participant-day and the unique key is ID plus calendar date. In part4_nightsummary, one participant can contribute several nights. One row therefore represents one participant-night and the key is ID plus night.


01:42 Finally, part5_personsummary is participant-level. Each row represents one participant, so ID should again be unique. These observation units determine which cleaning and merging operations are appropriate. Checking the key first prevents duplicated rows, silent inflation of the


01:58 dataset, and incorrect summaries later in the workflow. GGIR file names contain important information about how the data were processed. The part5_personsummary prefix tells us that this is a participant-level output created in Part 5. The letters WW mean wake to wake.


02:18 This identifies the definition of a day used for this output. L40, M100, and V400 record the light, moderate, and vigorous acceleration thresholds. T5 records the time threshold and A5 records the angle threshold. Together, these blocks identify the processing settings that produce the file.


02:38 Our project uses L40, M100, V400, T5, and A5. Do not replace these values with thresholds from a generic example. If the settings change, the file name and resulting measures may no longer be directly comparable. Reading the file name before importing the data helps us select the correct


02:57 source file and prevents us from combining outputs created with different settings. Before applying an exclusion, inspect cleaningcode. In this GGIR 3.3.6 course run, sleep_full contains 40 participant-night records: 33 have cleaningcode 1


03:14 and 7 have cleaningcode 2. With no sleep log, the project codebook says to exclude codes 2 through 6 for this demonstration; all 7 exclusions have code 2. This is course-specific, not a universal GGIR rule. Always preserve the original source


03:33 and save the cleaned records as a new traceable file. Now let's apply this rule in Stata. This recording demonstrates the verified module 6 workflow in a series of short, auditable steps. We begin with the full part 4 night summary. After importing the file,


03:51 we confirm the required variables and verify that participant ID plus night uniquely identifies every row. Before applying any exclusion, we examine the distribution of cleaningcode. This GGIR 3.3.6 sleep_full course run has 40 night records;


04:10 7 have cleaningcode 2. With no sleep log and after confirming the project codebook, the approved course rule removes codes 2 through 6. We then verify that the number of records before cleaning equals the number removed plus the number remaining. The


04:26 cleaned night-level data are saved as a new file while the original GGIR source remains unchanged. Next, we import the part 5 day summary. One additional participant-day has cleaning code 2 and is removed, leaving 31 participant-day records. The code then combines GGIR's mutually


04:45 exclusive bout intervals into cumulative measures. These include MVPA lasting at least 1, 5, and 10 minutes as well as inactivity lasting at least 20 minutes. We verify the expected nesting of these measures. For example, the 1 minute MVPA measure cannot be smaller than the 5 minute or 10 minute


05:04 measure. Finally, the participant identifier, calendar date, variable names, labels, and measurement units are standardized. The workflow checks unique keys and missing values, saves cleaned Stata and CSV files, and creates documentation for traceability. The final


05:21 screen shows the cleaned participant-day dataset. Module 7 will use these documented outputs to construct the final analysis dataset. GGIR reports bout duration using mutually exclusive bins. To create cumulative measures, we combine these existing bins in Stata. MVPA lasting at least 1


05:40 minute is the sum of the 1 to less than 5, 5 to less than 10, and 10 or more minute bins. MVPA lasting at least 5 minutes combines the last 2 bins, while MVPA lasting at least 10 minutes uses the 10 or more minute bin directly. Inactivity lasting at least 20 minutes combines


05:57 the 20 to less than 30 and 30 or more minute bins. These outcomes represent cumulative minutes per participant-day. Stata combines the GGIR outputs. It does not recreate bouts from the raw accelerometer signal. Finally, standardize the variable names while preserving their original meaning. For


06:18 example, ID becomes participant_id, calendar_date becomes activity_date, and cleaningcode becomes sleep_clean_code. The long GGIR bout variable dur_day_MVPA_bts_10_min is renamed mvpa_bout10_min. We then verify that participant ID and activity date form a unique key. The standardized dataset is exported in both


06:38 Stata and CSV formats. A data dictionary records the original and standardized names, source file, observation unit, measurement unit, transformation, missing data rule, and retention or exclusion decision. This creates a clear and reproducible record of every processing step.




Next Final Dataset in Stata

Cleaning should preserve traceability. Every standardized variable should point back to a source file and a processing decision.

title: Accelerometer Learning Course
text:
Skip to main content











 University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign / LA PASSSTA Lab


University research workflow · Self-paced


Turn raw movement signals into reproducible evidence.


Learn the complete accelerometer workflow—from study decisions and device deployment to quality review and an analysis-ready dataset.


Begin the course Explore the modules





8guided stages from concepts to final check


10captioned videos with summaries and transcripts


1downloadable toolkit for hands-on practice





The team behind the course


Course creators


The LA PASSSTA Lab—Longitudinal Analysis in Physical Activity, Sleep, Sitting, Screen Time, and Accelerometry—studies how movement behaviors influence health outcomes across the life course. As part of the Illini Physical Activity Initiative and coordinated by Dr. Otávio Leão, it offers a collaborative space where researchers, students, and other contributors advance health knowledge and promote well-being.



Course creatorOtávio Leão

Assistant Professor, Department of Kinesiology and Community HealthUniversity of Illinois Urbana-Champaign



Course creatorEric Li

PhD student



Course creatorMaynor Antonio Antonio







Why this course


Build the evidence trail—not just the output.


Accelerometers record acceleration, not ready-made measures of activity, sedentary behavior, or sleep. Credible results depend on the decisions made before, during, and after data collection.


This course connects those decisions into one practical workflow: define the protocol, preserve traceability, process raw files, interrogate data quality, and deliver a dataset another analyst can understand. Examples use ActiGraph, GGIR in R, and Stata, while the underlying principles extend beyond any one tool.







Your browser does not support the video tag. You can download the welcome video from this link.


Welcome video for the Accelerometer Learning Course.




Quick summary Brief review


This course follows accelerometer data from study planning and device deployment through downloading, organization, GGIR processing, quality control, cleaning, and creation of an analysis-ready Stata dataset. Throughout the workflow, study-specific decisions and reproducible documentation are treated as essential.





Read the full video transcript Timestamped · English


Download English captions (.vtt)



00:00 Welcome to the Accelerometer Learning Course. Accelerometers are powerful research tools because they let us move beyond self-report and observe patterns of movement, rest, and sleep over time. But


00:13 collecting accelerometer data is only the beginning. To turn a device recording into a trustworthy research dataset, every step has to be planned, documented, and checked. This course gives you a practical workflow for doing that work


00:28 from start to finish. We begin with the core concepts. What does an accelerometer record? What kinds of outcomes can it support? Why do device placement and study protocol matter? Then we move into the hands-on workflow. Accelerometry


00:44 turns raw movement into insight about how people move, rest, and sleep. Over eight modules, you'll learn the complete workflow. Module 1 introduces the accelerometer—what it records, and how placement shapes the data. Module 2


00:57 covers programming and downloading the device. Module 3, organizing and converting your files. Module 4 sets up R and GGIR to process the data. Module 5 checks data quality. Module 6 cleans and standardizes the output. Module 7 builds


01:13 the final dataset in Stata. And Module 8 is a knowledge check to consolidate what you've learned. After that, we show how raw device files can be converted and processed. The course uses ActiLife, R, GGIR, and Stata as the main examples.


01:29 These tools help move the data from raw acceleration signals into interpretable summaries of physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep-wake patterns. Just as important, you will learn how to inspect data quality. A single summary


01:45 number can hide problems, so the course emphasizes visual checks, clear decision rules, and careful notes about exclusions or concerns. By the end of the course, you should understand the complete path from planning and deploying


01:57 an accelerometer to preparing an analysis-ready dataset. You will also know where protocol decisions must be adapted for the population, device, wear location, and research question in your own study. This course is designed for


02:12 students, research assistants, and lab members who want a clear, reproducible introduction to accelerometer-based measurement. Start with the first module, accelerometer introduction, and then follow the workflow step-by-step. Welcome


02:25 to the course.







Choose your route


Learn the logic, then decide how far to practise it.



3–4 hoursConcept route

Read the lessons, watch the videos or use their transcripts, and complete the self-checks. A web browser is sufficient.



6–9 hoursHands-on route

Add every mini-activity and save the stated deliverables. Timing excludes software installation and full-dataset processing.




Hands-on prerequisites: Bring an approved or fictional study protocol and a safe practice dataset with no direct identifiers. Modules 2–3 require access to a compatible ActiGraph device and ActiLife for the demonstrated workflow. Modules 4–6 use R, RStudio, and GGIR. Module 7 uses Stata. ActiLife and Stata access may depend on your laboratory or institution’s licensing. Record the exact device, firmware, and software versions used in your own project.





Who can use this course


Built for learners and teams who work with movement data.


The concept route is suitable for beginners with a web browser. The hands-on route is for learners who also have access to an approved or fictional protocol, safe practice data, and the demonstrated software or devices.



StudyUndergraduate and graduate students

Build a foundation in accelerometry for kinesiology, public health, epidemiology, data science, or related coursework and research.



Research operationsResearch assistants and study teams

Use a shared workflow for device deployment, file traceability, quality review, and preparation of analysis-ready data.



Teaching and leadershipFaculty, instructors, and investigators

Support methods teaching, laboratory onboarding, protocol planning, and review of reproducible research practices.



PracticeHealth and movement professionals

Understand how wearable data are collected and interpreted in public health, clinical, exercise, and human-movement settings.



AnalysisData analysts and methodologists

Connect raw-device decisions with GGIR processing, quality-control evidence, documented cleaning, and final datasets.



IndustryCompany and consulting teams

Develop shared literacy for work in wearable technology, digital health, occupational health, research services, and related fields.









Module-by-module


Follow the workflow in order, with a useful output at every stage.


Begin with Module 1



Design · Module 1 · 50–70 minAccelerometer IntroductionTurn a research question into a draft device, placement, and wear-protocol decision.


Capture · Module 2 · 30–45 minProgramming and DownloadingCreate a reconciled initialization and download record from an approved protocol.


Trace · Module 3 · 25–40 minOrganizing and ConvertingProduce a folder map, naming rule, and documented conversion decision.

Questions before you begin


Frequently asked questions


Find the practical details first, then review the decisions that must be adapted for your own study.


Getting started




Who is this course for?


It is designed for undergraduate and graduate students; research assistants, coordinators, and laboratory teams; faculty, instructors, and investigators; public-health, clinical, exercise, and movement professionals; data analysts and methodologists; and company or consulting teams working in wearable technology, digital health, occupational health, or research services. The concept route is beginner-friendly, while the hands-on route requires appropriate software, devices, and safe practice data.




How long does the course take?


Allow about 3–4 hours for the concept route or 6–9 hours for the hands-on route. Full-dataset processing, software installation, and protocol approval take additional time. Each module card shows a planning estimate.




Which devices and software does the course use?


The examples use ActiGraph devices, ActiLife, GGIR in R, and Stata. You can complete the concept route in a browser. Hands-on work requires appropriate software and a safe practice dataset; access to ActiLife and Stata may depend on your laboratory or institution’s licensing.




Do I need previous experience with R, GGIR, or Stata?


No prior experience is required for the concept route. For the hands-on route, you should be comfortable finding files, editing paths, running a script, reading software messages, and protecting participant data. Basic familiarity with R and Stata is helpful in Modules 4–7.




How can I use the videos accessibly?


Each video is followed by a quick summary, a full transcript, and a downloadable caption track. The summary is for rapid review; it is not a substitute for the transcript or captions. Software controls and visual-only details are described in the accompanying text where they affect the task.




How do I know that I completed a module?


Complete the self-check and compare your reasoning with the feedback. On the hands-on route, also save the module’s stated deliverable—for example, a protocol decision, download log, GGIR configuration, QC log, or analysis script.




Methods and files




What does an accelerometer measure directly?


It records acceleration over time, usually along three axes. Behaviors such as activity intensity, sedentary time, posture, and sleep are estimates derived from the raw signal using a documented algorithm, wear location, and protocol.




Does GGIR require conversion from .gt3x to .csv?


No. GGIR can read .gt3x files directly. Convert to CSV only when a downstream script, another software package, data-sharing requirement, or audit workflow specifically needs it.




What is the difference between .gt3x and .agd files?


A .gt3x file contains raw ActiGraph acceleration data. The demonstrated workflow also creates a 10-second .agd, a count-based epoch summary that may be useful for ActiLife review or legacy workflows. Follow the approved protocol if it specifies another epoch length.




What counts as a valid participant record?


The course example uses at least 4 valid days, at least 10 hours of awake wear per valid day, and at least 1 weekend day. These are example rules and must be approved for the study population, device, placement, and protocol.




Are the course thresholds and cleaning rules universal?


No. Device settings, valid-day rules, intensity thresholds, wear criteria, and variable-specific cleaning rules are study-specific examples. Confirm every rule against the approved protocol, the exact software version, and the relevant output dictionary before applying it.




What should the final analysis package contain?


Include a dated .dta file, data dictionary, cleaning log, exclusion table, Stata do-file, and a README that identifies the source GGIR run and processing batches.








Ready when you are

Module 1 turns that question into the first documented device, placement, and wear-protocol decisions. You can return to the toolkit and transcripts at any point.

Module 8


Knowledge Checking


Check whether you can apply the course workflow, not just remember vocabulary, before using real study data.


File types QC decisions Study rules






Learning outcomes


By the end of this module, you should be able to:


Identify the correct file type for each processing step.
Choose complementary QC outputs and interpret key fields accurately.
Match GGIR parameters, bout settings, windows, and output names to their meanings.
Select safe merge keys and apply study-specific eligibility rules without erasing audit evidence.
Identify what must still be checked before using a course example on real data.










Plan this module
What you need




Estimated time
25–35 minutes


Prerequisites
Modules 1–7 and access to your pilot script, QC log, inventory, and data dictionary


Inputs
Your own course artifacts; no identifiable study data are needed


Output
Completed self-checks and a readiness decision: ready, revise, or seek review


Completion criterion
You can justify each answer and identify the exact document or file that supports it





Scored checkpoint Applied cases Short-answer review Readiness decision



Interactive self-check


Scored Workflow Checkpoint

Choose one answer for every question, then select Check answers. Feedback appears below each item. A score of 6/8 is a suggested review checkpoint, not a certification or research approval.


1 Which file is the appropriate raw ActiGraph input for the GGIR workflow demonstrated in this course?  A. A 10-second .agd file  B. A compatible raw .gt3x file  C. A participant-level Stata file  D. A PDF visual report




2 GGIR documentation describes six computational parts. What should a routine run use?  A. Always mode = 1:6  B. Only Part 6  C. The approved configuration—commonly mode = 1:5—with Part 6 added only when justified  D. Whichever mode produces the largest number of output files




3 What does complete_24hcycle represent?  A. A Boolean marker for one complete calendar day  B. A recording-level completeness score  C. A sleep-cleaning code  D. The number of days that meet the study’s valid-day rule




4 Which Part 5 per-recording report supports current quality review?  A. report…  B. old_report…  C. Either one, because they are identical  D. visualisation_sleep.pdf for every Part 5 review




5 Two Part 5 files use different L/M/V thresholds. What is the defensible next step?  A. Append them because the column names match  B. Keep whichever file is larger  C. Trace each configuration and keep methods separate unless a pre-specified analysis says otherwise  D. Average the two sets of thresholds and relabel both files




6 How should a day-level table be joined to a participant-level table?  A. Many-to-many on participant ID  B. Verify both keys, then many-to-one from day records to participant records  C. Drop duplicate participant IDs from the day table first  D. Join on row number after sorting both files




7 When is an additional sleep-record exclusion based on numbered cleaning codes justified?  A. Whenever a code is greater than 1  B. Whenever the record looks unusual  C. When the exact field, codebook, software version, and pre-specified rule support it  D. Whenever excluding the record improves the study result




8 Are ≥4 valid days, ≥10 awake-wear hours per day, and ≥1 weekend day universal GGIR defaults?  A. No, they are course-example study rules  B. Yes, for every population and placement  C. Yes, whenever Part 5 is run  D. Yes, whenever at least seven calendar days were planned





Check answers


Reset and retry






JavaScript is off, so interactive scoring and saved quiz progress are unavailable. Review the corresponding course sections and explanations with an instructor or peer.






Application


Applied Cases



1 A returned monitor appears to contain less than half of the planned collection period. What should happen before GGIR processing?  A. Delete the file immediately because it can never contribute usable evidence  B. Preserve it and follow the approved operational triage path, such as INCOMPLETE, without treating that as the final eligibility decision  C. Rename it COMPLETE so it enters routine processing without review  D. Replace the planned period in the protocol with the observed period




2 You find the course/project L40/M100/V400 file and another Part 5 file with different L/M/V values. How should they be handled?  A. Append them because both came from Part 5  B. Keep the larger file and discard the configuration records  C. Average the outcomes row by row to remove the threshold difference  D. Trace both configurations and keep the methods separate unless a pre-specified sensitivity analysis compares them




3 data_quality_report.csv has a calibration warning, but the current report… PDF looks broadly plausible. Is the recording automatically acceptable?  A. Yes, because a visual report always overrides numeric QC fields  B. Yes, if no participant complaint was recorded  C. No; reconcile all calibration, summary, plot, configuration, and field evidence and record a review decision  D. No; permanently exclude it without reviewing any other evidence




4 A person-level file has one row per participant, and a day-level file has several rows per participant. Which merge checks come first?  A. Define the target grain, verify each file’s full key separately, then use the explicit many-to-one relationship and inspect unmatched records  B. Use a many-to-many merge on participant ID and check the row count afterward  C. Drop all repeated participant IDs from the day-level file  D. Sort both files alphabetically and merge by row position




5 A participant fails both the valid-day and weekend requirements. Why should the do-file retain separate flags?  A. To count the same participant twice in the final sample  B. To show overlapping reasons, audit each rule, and support approved revisions from a saved pre-exclusion dataset  C. To avoid stating the final combined eligibility rule  D. To replace the need for an exclusion table





Check answers


Reset and retry








Review


Short-Answer Review

Choose the best answer to each review question, then use the feedback to revisit any uncertain distinction.


1 What is the difference between a raw signal and an activity outcome?  A. They are two names for the same directly measured behavior  B. A raw signal is already classified as MVPA, while an outcome contains the original sensor samples  C. A raw signal is recorded acceleration over time; an outcome is a processed estimate derived with documented methods  D. A raw signal exists only in Stata, while an outcome exists only in GGIR




2 Why does device placement affect interpretation?  A. Placement changes the captured motion and therefore the appropriate algorithms, thresholds, and interpretations  B. Placement matters only for participant comfort, never for the signal  C. Every validated hip threshold transfers directly to wrist data  D. Placement changes only the filename, not the analytical method




3 Why is conversion from .gt3x to .csv pipeline-dependent?  A. Every GT3X file must be converted before GGIR can read it  B. CSV conversion automatically improves signal quality  C. Conversion is needed whenever the raw filename contains a date  D. GGIR can read compatible GT3X files directly, so conversion is needed only for a documented downstream requirement




4 How does a recording-level completeness score differ from a day-level valid-day rule?  A. The two measures are interchangeable whenever their numeric values are similar  B. The score summarizes recording-wide cycle coverage; the valid-day rule evaluates each day using approved day-level fields and criteria  C. The score is a sleep code, while the valid-day rule is a file format  D. The score always counts weekdays, while the valid-day rule always counts weekends




5 Why should exclusion rules be decided before examining study associations?  A. Pre-specification reduces bias and makes the analytic sample defensible  B. It guarantees that no participant will ever be excluded  C. It removes the need to document overlapping exclusion reasons  D. It ensures every association will be statistically significant




6 What evidence would justify creating a Stata bout variable instead of using a GGIR bout output?  A. The Stata variable can be created with fewer lines of code  B. The analyst prefers a different variable name  C. The required construct is absent or intentionally different, with its resolution, metric, threshold, duration, interruption/non-wear rules, and validation documented  D. The GGIR output contains any missing value





Check answers


Reset and retry






Capstone mini-activity: audit your own pipeline


1 Which trace demonstrates that the capstone pipeline is auditable?  A. A final variable name with no link to the raw file or configuration  B. A verbal explanation from the original analyst without written evidence  C. A raw filename and final dataset row, with missing QC and exclusion steps left unmarked  D. A written link from raw filename through manifest, configuration, QC, inventory, dictionary, and exclusion evidence to the final variable, with gaps marked and independently repeatable





Check answer


Reset and retry









Final reflection


Make a Readiness Decision

Before using real study data, classify the pipeline as ready, revise, or seek review. “Ready” requires that you can show—not merely describe—the following:

the compatible input type and immutable source inventory,
the exact R/GGIR versions, time zones, script, and resolved config.csv,
pilot confirmation of ID extraction and expected outputs,
numeric, visual, and operational QC evidence with reviewer decisions,
the distinction between current QC reports and legacy reports,
the cleaned/full Part 4 sleep-file roles,
the configured thresholds, windows, and bout definitions,
asserted source keys and an explicit merge relationship,
pre-specified valid-day and exclusion flags with overlap counts,
a reproducible final dataset, log, dictionary, README, and release date.

Choose revise if any item is incomplete but can be resolved by updating the script or documentation. Choose seek review when the issue changes the scientific estimand, population-specific cut-points, sleep interpretation, or data eligibility rule.

Finish Course Completion

Use the readiness checklist, download the toolkit, and complete the synthetic capstone before adapting the workflow to a real study.

text:
Skip to main content







Course home

Module 4


Setting Up R and GGIR


Prepare an auditable R/GGIR workspace and learn how one documented GGIR() call turns raw files into quality-control, activity, and sleep outputs.


R/RStudio setup GGIR parts 1–6 Processing parameters






Learning outcomes


By the end of this module, you should be able to:


Prepare R/RStudio and a project-specific GGIR workspace.
Describe GGIR’s six numbered processing/reporting parts.
Adapt and pilot a documented GGIR() call using current parameter names.
Preserve the configuration, software versions, and pilot evidence needed to reproduce a run.










Plan this module
What you need




Estimated time
35–45 minutes, plus the time needed to process one pilot file


Prerequisites
Modules 1–3; permission to use a non-sensitive test file; basic R script editing


Inputs
One representative raw file, the study wear protocol, an agreed ID rule, and writable input/output folders


Output
A dated GGIR script, config.csv, session information, and a short pilot-run record


Completion criterion
You can explain every non-default argument and locate the pilot outputs without relying on memory





4.1 Software environment 4.2 GGIR parts 4.3 Core parameters 4.4 Preserve the run 4.5 Practice and self-check



Lesson 4.1


Install and Document the Software Environment

GGIR is an R package that processes raw accelerometer recordings into summaries that can support physical-activity, inactivity, sleep, and circadian-rhythm analyses. Use the central GGIR() function as the user-facing entry point; it coordinates the numbered parts of the pipeline.
Official software links:

R: https://cran.r-project.org/
RStudio: https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/
GGIR documentation: https://wadpac.github.io/GGIR/
GGIR parameter reference: https://wadpac.github.io/GGIR/articles/GGIRParameters.html
GGIR CRAN page: https://cran.r-project.org/package=GGIR

Install GGIR in R:
install.packages("GGIR")
Before running GGIR, record:

R version,
GGIR version,
time zone,
device type and placement,
input folder,
output folder,
operator,
date of processing,
approved protocol parameters.


Course example: Pelotas/UFPel cohort Use a dedicated project folder with separate subfolders for raw .gt3x files, GGIR output, QC review, and Stata files. Keep the exact GGIR() call used for each processing run in a dated script, even when only one argument changes.


Three levels of guidance: Reproducibility, explicit time zones, and preserving source files are general principles. The behavior and defaults of GGIR parameters are software-version dependent. Thresholds, wear rules, sleep-log handling, and ID extraction are study decisions. Never copy the course values into a real study without checking all three levels.




Lesson 4.2


GGIR’s Six Numbered Parts

GGIR’s current documentation describes six sequential computational parts. The default mode = 1:5 runs the first five parts; part 6 is optional and is described in the parameter reference as under development. Do not request part 6 merely because it exists.









Part
Current role in the official pipeline
Practical implication




Part 1
Load data, assess signal quality, and store derived metrics such as ENMO for later parts.
Changing raw-data or metric settings requires reconsidering downstream outputs.


Part 2
Assess basic data quality and describe data per day, file, and optional day segment.
Produces person/day summaries and core QC material.


Part 3
Estimate rest periods used by part 4.
Required when the analysis needs the later sleep classifications.


Part 4
Label rest periods as sleep and summarize sleep by night and recording.
Produces cleaned and full sleep summaries with different purposes.


Part 5
Combine earlier information, classify sleep and physical-behavior categories, detect bouts, and produce day/person summaries.
Threshold and bout settings become part of the analysis method and output names.


Part 6
Support analyses spanning the full recording, including selected co-analysis and circadian-rhythm functionality.
Optional; use only for a pre-specified question and verify the installed version’s documentation.





Official source: See The GGIR pipeline. Output reports and milestone files are not interchangeable: milestone .RData files connect GGIR parts internally, while user-facing CSV, PNG, and PDF files are stored under results.




Lesson 4.3


Core GGIR Parameters

The values below form one coherent course/project configuration, not a recommendation for a particular population. It uses L40/M100/V400 throughout modules 4–8; these values also match the current GGIR defaults, but that coincidence does not make them universally valid. Replace the ID rule, time zone, protocol masking, thresholds, and sleep settings only after documenting the study rationale.
library(GGIR)

input_dir <- "03_ggir_input"
output_dir <- "04_ggir_output"

GGIR(
  datadir = input_dir,
  outputdir = output_dir,
  mode = 1:5,
  idloc = 1,                 # Teaching placeholder: verify against file names
  desiredtz = "America/Sao_Paulo",
  do.enmo = TRUE,
  data_masking_strategy = 1,
  hrs.del.start = 0,
  hrs.del.end = 0,
  maxdur = 0,
  qwindow = c(0, 24),
  mvpadur = c(1, 5, 10),     # Part 2 MVPA bout durations
  timethreshold = 5,
  anglethreshold = 5,
  def.noc.sleep = 1,
  threshold.lig = 40,
  threshold.mod = 100,
  threshold.vig = 400,
  boutcriter.mvpa = 0.8,
  boutcriter.in = 0.9,
  boutdur.mvpa = c(1, 5, 10),
  boutdur.in = 20,
  timewindow = c("MM", "WW"),
  visualreport = TRUE,
  old_visualreport = FALSE
)
idloc = 1 is only a visible placeholder in this template. Confirm how GGIR extracts IDs from the actual file names during the pilot and change it when needed. The example time zone is appropriate only when both device configuration and data collection occurred in that zone; consult configtz when they differed.









Parameter
What it controls
Decision to document




datadir
Folder containing input accelerometer files, usually raw .gt3x for this course.
Which batch/folder was processed.


outputdir
Folder where GGIR writes results and reports.
Where outputs are archived and reviewed.


mode
Which GGIR parts to run; the documented default is 1:5.
